items.title: Engineers… Your Software Factory NEEDS Agent Sandboxes to SCALE (exe.dev)
items.summary: Engineers... if you're IN the loop, you ARE the bottleneck. 🔥 And giving your agents a tiny corner of YOUR computer is why your software factory can't scale past one. 🎥 VIDEO REFERENCES • Factory In A Box Codebase: https://github.com/disler/inkwell-agent-sandboxes-and-software-factory • Super Simple Software Factory Video: https://youtu.be/haUfb1ievTE • FORGET Loop Engineering Video: https://youtu.be/VQy50fuxI34 • Agent Sandboxes on Exe.dev: https://exe.dev/ • OpenRouter provisioning keys API: https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/overview/auth/management-api-keys PUSH YOUR AGENTIC CODING BEYOND Tactical Agentic Coding: https://agenticengineer.com/tactical-agentic-coding?y=SEI_qIW4o2c Stop renting your machine to your agents. Give every agent its own computer. N agents, N environments, zero collisions. That's what an agent sandbox unlocks: isolation, scale, autonomy. 🚀 In this video we put the entire software factory INSIDE an agent sandbox. Not one agent in the cloud, the whole factory: the AI developer workflow, the agent configs, the app, and an orchestrator agent, all living on a machine that isn't yours. One prompt from Claude Code fires off five sandboxes on exe.dev, each running the full software developer life cycle against the same prompt. Best of N, five futures, one pick. 🛠️ The three tier architecture is the unlock. items.excerpt: # Chrome DevTools for agents [![npm chrome-devtools-mcp package](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/chrome-devtools-mcp.svg)](https://npmjs.org/package/chrome-devtools-mcp) Chrome DevTools for agents (`chrome-devtools-mcp`) lets your coding agent (such as Antigravity, Claude, Cursor or Copilot) control and inspect a live Chrome browser. It acts as a Model-Context-Protocol (MCP) server, giving your AI coding assistant access to the full power of Chrome DevTools for reliable automation, in-depth debugging, and performance analysis. A [CLI][cli] is also provided for use without MCP. [Tool reference][tool-reference] | [Changelog][changelog] | [Contributing][contributing] | [Troubleshooting][troubleshooting] | [Design Principles][design-principles] ## Key features - **Get performance insights**: Uses [Chrome DevTools](https://github.com/ChromeDevTools/devtools-frontend) to record traces and extract actionable performance insights. - **Advanced browser debugging**: Analyze network requests, take screenshots and check browser console messages (with source-mapped stack traces). - **Reliable automation**. Uses [puppeteer](https://github.com/puppeteer/puppeteer) to automate actions in Chrome and automatically wait for action results. ## Disclaimers `chrome-devtools-mcp` exposes content of the browser instance to the MCP clients allowing them to inspect, debug, and modify any data in the browser or DevTools. items.title: akitaonrails / ai-memory
items.summary: Solution for long term memory for agent coding CLIs and to facilitate handoff between different agent vendors
items.excerpt: > Long-term memory for AI coding agents. Quit Claude Code mid-task, > start OpenAI Codex in the same directory, continue without > re-explaining the architecture, the failed approaches, or the open > questions. [![Release](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/akitaonrails/ai-memory)](https://github.com/akitaonrails/ai-memory/releases/latest) [![Rust](https://img.shields.io/badge/rust-1.95+-blue)](rust-toolchain.toml) [![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-blue)](LICENSE) ## Why ai-memory Your coding agent already has a memory feature. Claude Code takes its own notes, Cursor remembers some things, and every platform is adding more. All of them share the same walls: the notes live on one machine, belong to one agent, and vanish from view the moment you switch tools — or teammates. ai-memory is what's on the other side of those walls. - **It follows you across agents.** Twenty-plus harnesses — Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, Grok, Devin, Kimi, Kiro, and more — feed one shared memory. Quit Claude Code mid-task, open Codex in the same directory, and the next agent picks up a real handoff: where you left off, what failed, what's still open. Handoffs are a protocol here, not a convention — typed, owned, claimed exactly once. - **It follows you across machines.** Memory lives in a server you run — on the same laptop, a homelab box, or wherever — so the project you left on the desktop is the project you resume on the laptop. items.title: FIXING Opus 5: PROOF that Prompt Engineering IS NOT DEAD
items.summary: Opus 5 is one of the BEST models ever released, and one of the WORST to talk to. Verbose, "load-bearing" everywhere, torching your output tokens. So we FIX it with the skill everyone said was dead: PROMPT ENGINEERING. 🔥 🎥 VIDEO REFERENCES • Fix Opus 5 Codebase: https://github.com/disler/fixing-smartass-opus-5 • Software Factory (Advanced): https://youtu.be/haUfb1ievTE • Zucks Post: https://www.meta.com/thefutureisforeveryone/?srsltid=AfmBOoqCUQLgMU5sfTup2SoH9ZpFlQ_wwSMLzccQkoziF-mR5iiDExgI PUSH YOUR AGENTIC ENGINEERING BEYOND Tactical Agentic Coding: https://agenticengineer.com/tactical-agentic-coding?y=S_QdQ1G4GlU 🚀 In this video, IndyDevDan turns smartass Claude Opus 5 into a precise senior engineer with SYSTEM prompt engineering. There are two ways to prompt your AI coding agents: the user prompt (one task) and the system prompt (the LAW for every task). Most engineers fixate on the user prompt and skills. The real leverage is the system prompt, where every word you write gets multiplied over every single prompt in and every response out of Claude Code. 🛠️ Key takeaways: Positive + Negative Patterns: Tell your agent exactly what to replicate and exactly what to avoid (goodbye "load bearing", "worth stating plainly", em dash chains). Reference Points: Encode D1/R1/F1 style codes so you and your agent build a fast shared language and stop repeating tokens. Hard Operational Boundaries: Deliver ONLY what was requested. No scope creep, no surprise refactors, no co-author…

items.summary: Vinny is back on the pod, and he explains WebMCP. WebMCP puts MCP tools inside the browser UI, so any agent that you bring can read a page and act on it. Vinny demos an espresso gear store where his agent compares two machines, checks the counter width, matches accessories, adds an item to the cart, and applies a coupon. Together we map the agent-native options, from headless APIs to in-app agents, and we place WebMCP in the middle of that map. I close the episode with two cash-flowing business ideas that a semi-technical founder can start today.
